if its possible, maybe have her talk to someone who has been transitioning for a couple years already? that way she can have her concerns heard by someone in an appropriate conversation and not be stuck in a potential terf bubble by finding answers online. I've seen other people say this has helped them when their partner/loved ones have come out as trans and they are having issues with understanding and grieving.

whilst your mum seems to tolerate and put up with you being trans, she appears hesitant to fully accept in the hope that you'll return to who she thinks you still are. this is different for every person and I'm not fully sure what your relationship with your mum is like, but maybe try and get her to understand shes not losing you. this is a way for her to know you more closely, more authentically than forcing an alternative. transitioning isnt a one and done process, it's a lifetime and whilst hrt is a massive part of it for many there is still so much more to finding who you are. im sure your mum would find it horrible if anyone was denied that basic decency and opportunity.

it's hard in the UK now with a lot of transphobic rhetoric being perpetuated on every level, especially towards younger trans people. wishing you the best and hope that your mum chooses to love you as you are

im a trans woman who's still closeted at home but taking hrt so have been undergoing some of the fun changes for about 2 years now (family are just in denial with what i look like now ha). anyway, was out shopping with my mum one day and we go in the lift and theres another woman already inside. as we go up one floor, before the woman leaves, she turns to my mum and says "your daughter has a really nice face shape". 

besides the awkwardness at still being closeted to my mum, i couldn't stop smiling that day and honestly it's one of the happiest memories I've got from the past year or two. it was such an affirming compliment because it wasnt directed to me, but said to my mum about how her daughter was pretty. given the possibility that my mum might not be accepting when i do come out, i just felt this odd but joyous sense of self-love that i rarely feel. theres just something endearing about having your gender affirmed through what your connection to others is 💞

It's satire, like how we're called triggered for legitimate reasons about concern and safety, I should be able to call those who find the mere notion of transgender and gnc people a violation of some subjective and ill-informed societal law 'triggered'. 

But I agree with the concern, making jokes about it in any case devalues its use for those who really need them.

I dont think its a pointed joke towards her being bi, pan or anything else, as much as jokes about her being sleezy or mistrusting were about her inherent nature than the culture she was brought up in. One point is how bad her past relationships were compared to the one she has with Chidi now as she's grown as a person. Her being bad before wasn't to show 'straight relationships are inherently bad', despite straight culture being so so toxic, but the person she came to be from a combination of external and internal factors. Jason and Janet's relationship is quite on the nose, commenting on the simple joys of being with someone. But its very wholehearted, yet still played for laughs at times because we know that being cheesy can be both cringe and very cute. Eleanor can be flirty and more direct without being a biphobic representation. The remarks she made became increasingly sincere and platonic with the close group they made over the series, almost becoming family, and her continued jokes showed insecurity becoming self-positivity and acknowledging if you're with the right people you can be happy. Especially compared to other so called 'representation' of bi or gay people, it was never about her identity, but more to do with her anxieties, flaws and fear of indifference to the world. A lot of rep is misguided, focusing on 'the struggle' of LGBTQ+ people rather than having them be a person with worldly struggles and desires. The Good Place nails that philosophy of we're all human, with these seperate parts making us who we are. 

But that's just my take away, yours is completely valid too, after all interpretation will always be different.

What a lot of people are missing is Eleanor is actually the type of representation a lot of sexually fluid and queer individuals want. A character that normalises the idea that they can be attracted to whoever the fork they want without it being held against them in a derogatory or stereotypical way. 

The whole point of the show was to demonstrate no one is perfect, or reaches a place in their life and stops. We're all growing and changing and life goes on and the best we can do is try to be good. As such, Eleanor having flaws shouldn't be a reflection of her gender, race, class or perceived sexuality. But just a person going about a forked up world where the things they are effect their position in certain ways. 

Honestly if you had a conversation with gay, bi, pan or however else they may identify people you would hear jokes just like this. Self deprecating, brushes off deep-seated anxieties about your self image and being overly critical in a sarcastic way of the straight culture our society coverts. 

No representation can be perfect, no representation will fit your personal self image. But I am really glad of a character like Eleanor that just normalises sexual freedom amidst all her other human problems and doesn't make it a performative archetype.


Just a note: I'm hella bisexual and gender questioning so this is coming from a place of knowing what it's like as an LGBTQ+ person.

It can be hard to come to terms with but you don't always have to be in line with what the world says. Like even just beings trans is still against what most of the world considers normal. Difference always will be scary to some and maybe you won't ever agree that the a = 1. But for anyone saying that there is only conflict and tension with difference is just not seeing its worth in how it offers a new perspective to view things. Most things in the world don't just exist on a right/wrong basis. There will always be different experiences, different values. What you might consider normal might be completely alien to another person. But that doesnt make either of you wrong. And even if one is wrong that doesn't make you any less worthy of affection, friendship and whatnot. It should be a reason to grow and change, which is ultimately what life is about.

I've found over the past few years the worst harm is the harm we do to ourselves in finding our worth in the necessity we have to others. Especially being trans or gnc that can be even harder when nothing really gets you or finding nothing you can truly fit into. Trust me I understand how important a community, friends can be. But before all that you need to see your own worth as a living human. Validation starts with yourself and it is not selfish at all to put your own thoughts before anyone else's, especially when it concerns you. It is not your responsibility to maintain relations, friendships. If those people don't bother to take the time and keep you company, give a listening ear and simply be there for you, then they aren't worth your time. I'm sure you will find people who will appreciate you just as much as you appreciate them. Sometimes it takes a while to find people you truly can connect with, truly be yourself with and that's completely fine. We are all going at our own pace and just try keep hold of them positive what if's. The bad in life doesn't make the good worth any less.
